summary: Proposes rules for assigning Top-Level Aggregation and Next-Level Aggregation identifiers in the IPv6 aggregatable address format. It was a proposal for how address space would be handed out. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 addresses can be handed out so that a whole organisation's addresses sit under one route, which keeps the routing tables small. This memo sets out who may receive such an organisation-wide block, and the conditions they must meet. An organisation first gets a provisional allocation, and only receives a full one after it can show it is really carrying traffic for others.

subtitle: Rules for handing out the two identifier fields that let IPv6 routers group many sites under one route.

tldr.problem: The IPv6 aggregatable address format names an organisation in a 13-bit field and a site in a 24-bit field. Someone has to decide who gets which values, and under what conditions, or the global routing table grows beyond what routers can hold.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes a two-stage allocation. A registry first hands out a Sub-TLA ID carved out of TLA ID 0x0001, and a full TLA ID follows once the recipient shows it is running transit service and has used more than 90 percent of its NLA space.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and was written as input to IANA and the registries rather than as a standard. Its rules were intended for the first two years of IPv6 TLA assignments and were expected to change as routing technology and experience developed.

today: RFC 2450 is an Informational memo from December 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It was written as input to IANA and the registries rather than as a standard, and it says itself that its procedures were intended for the first two years of IPv6 TLA assignments and were expected to change.

sections.title: What the Memo Proposes
sections.content:
RFC 2450 proposes rules for handing out Top-Level Aggregation Identifiers (TLA ID) and Next-Level Aggregation Identifiers (NLA ID) as defined in RFC 2374. The rules apply to the registries that allocate TLA IDs and to the organisations that receive them.

The memo says plainly what it is and is not. It is intended as input from the IPng working group to IANA and the registries, and it is not intended to have any official IETF status. Its content represents the result of extensive discussion between the IPng working group, IANA and the registries.

The scope is the first two years of IPv6 TLA address assignments. The memo expects that the procedures it proposes may change as routing technology evolves and as more experience is gained with allocating IPv6 addresses.

The address format the rules apply to was designed to support both the current provider-based aggregation and a new type of exchange-based aggregation, so that routing aggregation works efficiently for sites that connect directly to providers and for sites that connect to exchanges. Sites get the choice of connecting to either kind of aggregation entity. The format does not depend on exchanges for its route aggregation properties: it provides efficient aggregation with provider-based aggregation alone.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is a proposal about who gets which block of IPv6 addresses, written to be handed to the people who do the handing out. It covers only the first two years of allocations and expects to be revised. The address format it describes was designed so that a group of sites can be announced as one route, whether the sites buy their connectivity from a provider or from an exchange.

sections.title: The Aggregatable Address Format
sections.content:
The IPv6 Aggregatable Global Unicast Address Format divides the 128-bit address into five fields of fixed width, plus one reserved field.

  • FP, a 3-bit Format Prefix whose value is 001, identifies aggregatable global unicast addresses.
  • TLA ID, 13 bits, is the Top-Level Aggregation Identifier.
  • RES, 8 bits, is reserved for future use.
  • NLA ID, 24 bits, is the Next-Level Aggregation Identifier.
  • SLA ID, 16 bits, is the Site-Level Aggregation Identifier.
  • Interface ID, 64 bits, identifies a single interface.

The first three fields, together 24 bits, form the part of the address that describes the public topology. The NLA ID and SLA ID together describe the site topology, and the Interface ID identifies one interface. Because the site fields have fixed sizes, every prefix that identifies a particular site is the same length, 48 bits, which is what makes it practical for a site to move in the topology, for example by changing service provider or by connecting to more than one provider at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is cut into fixed-width pieces. The first three, 24 bits together, say which part of the Internet the address belongs to. The next two say which site inside that part, and the last 64 bits identify one network interface. Because the site pieces are always the same width, a whole site can be moved to a different provider without changing the length of its routes.

sections.title: Why the Fields Were Sized That Way
sections.content:
The sizes of the fields were chosen to meet technical requirements set out in RFC 2374. The important constraint is the size of the default-free routing table in the Internet's top level routers.

A 13-bit TLA ID allows for 8,192 TLA IDs. The size was chosen so that the default-free routing table stays within the limits of current routing technology with a reasonable margin. The margin matters because default-free routers also carry a significant number of longer, more specific prefixes used to optimise paths inside a TLA and between TLAs. For comparison, the current IPv4 default-free routing table is approximately 50,000 prefixes. Whether that is already too many is a matter of debate, and there are serious issues of route stability and of providers not supporting all top level prefixes, so the requirement was to pick a TLA ID size below, with a reasonable margin, what IPv4 was doing.

The choice of 13 bits was an engineering compromise. Fewer bits would not support enough top level organisations; more bits would exceed what current routing technology can reasonably accommodate with a reasonable margin. If routing technology later improves, there are two ways to increase the number of TLA IDs: expand the TLA ID field into the reserved field, which would raise the number of TLA IDs to approximately 2 million, or allocate another format prefix for use with this address format. Either approach, or a combination, would allow the number of TLA IDs to increase significantly.

The 8-bit reserved field was sized to allow significant growth of either the TLA ID or the NLA ID field. The 24-bit NLA ID allows for approximately sixteen million NLA IDs if used in a flat manner, and, used hierarchically, a complexity roughly equivalent to the IPv4 address space, assuming an average network size of 254 interfaces. The 16-bit SLA ID supports 65,535 individual subnets per site, which was the goal for all but the largest of organisations; organisations needing more subnets can arrange with their provider to obtain additional site identifiers. The 64-bit Interface ID was chosen to meet the requirement to support EUI-64 based interface identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The 13 bits for the organisation field allow 8,192 organisations. That is deliberately fewer than the number of prefixes an IPv4 router already holds, because the Internet's top level routers will also carry more specific routes for the traffic inside each organisation. If the field later needs to grow, there is a spare 8-bit field reserved for exactly that.

sections.title: Rules for Assigning TLA IDs
sections.content:
TLA IDs are assigned to organisations providing transit topology. They are specifically not assigned to organisations only providing leaf topology. Assignment does not imply ownership, but it does imply stewardship over a valuable Internet resource.

The IAB and IESG have authorised IANA to manage the IPv6 address space. IANA assigns small blocks, for example a few hundred TLA IDs, to registries, and the registries assign the TLA IDs to organisations that meet the requirements. When a registry has used all of its TLA IDs it can ask IANA for another block, and the blocks do not have to be contiguous. IANA may also assign TLA IDs directly to organisations, including the temporary assignments used for testing and experimental activity such as the 6bone or new approaches such as exchanges.

Allocation happens in two stages. The first stage allocates a Sub-TLA ID. When the recipient has demonstrated that it has assigned more than 90 percent of the NLA IDs for its Sub-TLA ID, it is allocated a TLA ID. The Sub-TLA ID does not have to be returned. Sub-TLA IDs are assigned out of TLA ID 0x0001, and using the reserved field to create the Sub-TLA field is specific to TLA ID 0x0001 and does not affect any other TLA. A Sub-TLA allocation is interim until the organisation can show evidence of IPv6 Internet transit service; if transit service cannot be demonstrated by three months from the date of allocation, the allocation is revoked.

Registries enforce six requirements. The organisation must have a plan to offer native IPv6 service within 3 months of assignment, including NLA ID allocation and registration procedures, which may be subcontracted to another organisation such as a registry. It must have a verifiable track record of providing Internet transit to other organisations, verified by techniques such as traceroute and BGP advertisements, and must not be assigned a Sub-TLA or TLA ID if it only provides leaf service even if multihomed. It must pay a registration fee to IANA, with all fees paid before the assignment is made. It must provide registry services for the NLA ID space it is responsible for, covering both sites and next level providers, and the database of NLA assignments must be public and available to the registries. It must periodically provide utilisation statistics to the registry, along with evidence of carrying TLA routing and transit traffic, in the form of traffic statistics, traceroutes, routing table dumps or similar means. And an organisation asking for another Sub-TLA or TLA ID must show that it has assigned more than 90 percent of the NLA ID space in its previous allocations. An organisation that stops meeting these requirements may have custody revoked.
sections.plainLanguage: Only organisations that carry other people's traffic get one of these blocks. The process has two steps: a provisional smaller allocation first, and a full allocation once the organisation can show it is running transit service and has used up most of what it was given. If it cannot show that within three months, the allocation is taken back. Registries also check that the organisation keeps publishing its records and keeps proving it is carrying traffic.

sections.title: Rules for Assigning NLA IDs
sections.content:
NLA IDs are used by organisations holding a Sub-TLA ID or a TLA ID to create an addressing hierarchy and to identify sites. The organisation can assign the top part of the NLA ID in whatever way suits its own network.

Registries may initially assign only a fraction of the NLA ID space of a particular Sub-TLA or TLA ID. When the organisation has assigned more than 90 percent of that space it may request more. Organisations assigned a Sub-TLA or TLA ID are required to assume, directly or indirectly, the registry duties for the NLA IDs they assign: each organisation assigned an NLA ID must assume registry duties for the next level of NLA IDs it assigns, following the registry guidelines, and must pass that information back to the registry that assigned its TLA or Sub-TLA. The holder collects the information from the next level, the next level holder collects it from the level below, and so on.

The design of the bit layout of the NLA ID space for a given Sub-TLA or TLA ID is left to the organisation responsible for it, and the design of the next level of NLA IDs is the responsibility of the organisation assigned the previous level. The memo recommends that organisations assigning NLA address space use slow start allocation procedures, as is currently done with IPv4 CIDR blocks.

The design of an NLA ID allocation plan is a trade-off between routing aggregation efficiency and flexibility. Creating hierarchies allows for a greater amount of aggregation and results in smaller routing tables. Flat NLA ID assignment provides for easier allocation and attachment flexibility, but results in larger routing tables.
sections.plainLanguage: The organisation that holds the organisation-wide block decides how to divide it up among its own sites, and it takes on the job of keeping the records for the part it hands out, handing those records up to the registry that gave it the block. Grouping the sites into a tree keeps the routing tables small; handing out flat blocks is easier but produces more routes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security section is short and points elsewhere. IPv6 addressing documents do not have any direct impact on Internet infrastructure security, and authentication of IPv6 packets is defined in RFC 2402.

It does raise one related issue and sets it aside. Authenticating the ownership of prefixes, to avoid prefix stealing, is a security issue, but the memo says it is beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: How an address is allocated does not by itself affect the security of the Internet, and checking that an IPv6 packet really came from the sender it claims is covered elsewhere. One related problem, making sure nobody claims a prefix they do not own, is named here and left to other work.
